hypothesis: Batch-divergence threshold measures decision margin and would order representations on an axis perplexity and 4-gram cannot see. Proposed by me one step earlier.
REFUTED: The ordering is wrong. q2-g128-experts scores 12.7 -- HIGHER than q3-g128-experts at 2.7 -- while being the arm that emits 87 consecutive identical tokens and fails the gate on both terms. The passing representation looks WORSE on this metric than a destroyed one.
WHY_IT_IS_CONFOUNDED: A model locked in a repetition attractor is maximally STABLE under perturbation: it will re-emit the same token whatever the accumulation order. So a high margin score conflates 'far from decision boundaries' with 'stuck'. Degeneracy and robustness are indistinguishable to this measure, and degeneracy is exactly what the gate exists to catch.
ALSO_TOO_NOISY: n=3 prompts, and a single prompt surviving to B=16 contributes 32 to the mean, swinging it by ~10. bf16 itself ranges from B=4 to survival across three prompts.
NOT_ADOPTED: The metric is not added as a third gate axis. The one real observation behind it survives on its own: bf16 tolerates B=2 while q3-g128 does not, on the SAME prompt. That is a pairwise statement about two arms, not a scalar that orders a frontier.
WHAT_A_CORRECTED_VERSION_NEEDS: Condition on non-degeneracy: measure divergence only on prompts whose own B=1 output is already non-repetitive, so a locked model scores nothing rather than scoring well. That is a different metric and it is untested.
PROCESS_NOTE: Proposed, measured and refuted within one step, at a cost of four generations per arm. The constitution's 'when a result looks too good, attack it' applied to my own proposal.
